name: Ben Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ben, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Terry, who I was at school with. He's got a small firm, him, his nephew and me, doing extensions and loft conversions round town. Right now we're on a kitchen extension for a couple on Orchard Road, so I'm digging footings, mixing, barrowing blocks, and Terry's letting me do a bit of the stud work for the roof. I was a postman for thirty years before this, so I know every street, but I don't know much about building yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why did you leave the post?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They cut the rounds back, more parcels, fewer letters, and they offered money to anyone who'd go. I took it at fifty-six, and most of it went on a new boiler and helping our lad Dan when his marriage broke up. So now it's me and Carol, she works the counter at the chemist's, a small mortgage with six years left, and about three weeks of money in the bank. I've still got the same flip phone I had in the post. Never needed more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, all that fuss about nothing. I'm not one for posting online, I wouldn't know how. At work I'd say it to Terry over a tea, and he'd probably agree, he does his quotes on paper anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I just keep going, and that suits me. I've got six years on the mortgage and about seven till my pension, and I just want them quiet. If nothing changes, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up for Terry, keep learning the stud work, and that's it. Maybe put a bit by when there's a good month. I wouldn't do anything different because there'd be nothing to be different about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss out on if AI just stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not that I can think of. My daughter Lucy says it helps her at the bank with letters and such, so maybe she'd miss it. Me, I never used it, so you can't miss what you never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put a bit by in a good month. How often is there a good month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one in four. In summer, when Terry's got two jobs on, there's overtime and I might put a hundred by. Winter, it's rain days and no pay, so the hundred goes back out again.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, all that fuss about nothing. I'd say it to Terry over a tea, not online, because I don't post anything.
S0.think: I just keep going, and that suits me. I've got six years on the mortgage and about seven till my pension, and I just want them quiet.
S0.do: Keeps turning up for Terry's small extension firm and keeps learning stud work. Puts a bit by in good months and changes nothing else.
S0.quote: Winter, it's rain days and no pay, so the hundred goes back out again.
S0.fieldNote: Ben has never used AI and sees no reason to start; a stalled AI is simply no news for him. His horizon is short and concrete: mortgage and pension dates. He talks through his friendship with Terry rather than through politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it is what it is, things always change. I'd probably say to Terry, you'll have to learn it, mate, I'm too old. I wouldn't say much more than that, I'm not one for speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our sort of work, little extensions for people on Orchard Road, is the last place they'll send a robot. But Terry might start doing his quotes and his drawings on a tablet, and then what's he need a slow labourer for? I'm not worth much if the job gets quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder, be first in, last out, so Terry doesn't think twice. I wouldn't go on courses, honestly, I'd rather watch and see what happens to the big firms first. If it got bad, I'd ask Terry straight out where I stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like when the post started changing, before they offered the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Terry where you stood. What do you think he'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say don't be daft, Ben, you're fine. He's loyal, Terry, we go back forty-five years. But he's also got his nephew to think about, and the nephew's quicker than me with everything, so I'd know what loyalty's worth when the work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think about learning the tablet stuff yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I had thirty years of the post making me carry a scanner that beeped at me, and I hated every day of it. If Terry wants a tablet, that's Terry's business, I'll carry the blocks.

S1.say: I'd say it is what it is, things always change, and tell Terry he'll have to learn it because I'm too old. I'm not one for speeches, so I'd leave it at that.
S1.think: Little extensions like ours are the last place they'll send a robot, but if Terry does his quotes and drawings on a tablet, why keep a slow labourer? I'm not worth much if the job gets quicker.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and works harder, first in and last out, so Terry keeps him. Avoids courses, waits to see what happens to the big firms, and plans to ask Terry where he stands if it gets bad.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like the early days of changes at the post.
S1.quote: I'm not worth much if the job gets quicker.
S1.fieldNote: Ben's security rests on a forty-five-year friendship, and he knows it may not hold. He chooses effort over learning new tools. He sees change as weather, not anyone's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and someone in charge had better sort it. I don't blame anyone in particular, it's just how things go. But I'd want the government to do something, because I can't see what else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in a right state. I'm sixty in 2028, I've still got four years left on the mortgage, and Terry won't keep me on if a robot can dig footings. What am I going to do, go back to the post? They'll have robots there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Carol and look at every bill, cancel the sports channel, stop the car, sell my old van, that's maybe a couple of thousand. I'd ring the bank about the mortgage before I missed a payment. And I'd ask Lucy if she could help us out for a bit, much as I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted, really. Like someone's pulled the chair out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would asking Lucy for help feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Horrible. I've always been the one who helped them, the boiler, the money for Dan. Asking my own daughter for money, I'd rather dig footings in the rain for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Would you try anything new before it comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd just hang on. I'd tell Terry I'd work for a bit less if it kept me on longer, I would. Trying something new at fifty-nine, when everything's changing anyway, I wouldn't know where to start.

S2.say: I'd say that's that, and someone in charge had better sort it. I don't blame anyone in particular, but I'd want the government to do something.
S2.think: I'd be in a right state: sixty, four years left on the mortgage, and Terry won't keep me if a robot can dig footings. I can't go back to the post either, because they'll have robots too.
S2.do: Cuts bills with his wife, cancels the sports channel and sells his old van for a couple of thousand. Rings the bank about the mortgage before missing a payment and asks his daughter for help.
S2.feel: Gutted, as if someone pulled the chair out from under him.
S2.quote: Asking my own daughter for money, I'd rather dig footings in the rain for a month.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI turns Ben's quiet plan into an emergency. He doesn't blame anyone and wants the government to sort it, but his practical steps are about bills and family. Pride is his sore spot: he has always been the helper, not the one asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the government time to make a plan, so they'd better make one. Something for people my age who can't retrain. I'd say that to whoever asked, but I wouldn't go marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me to sixty-three, with the mortgage nearly done. If I can just keep Terry happy that long, it's doable, just about. It's tight, but it's not a cliff edge like the two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to pay the mortgage off early, an extra fifty a month, if I can find it. I'd stop buying lunch from the bakery and take sandwiches. And I'd keep going for Terry for as long as he wants me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see the end of the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do in those five years to make yourself harder to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'm not going to become a computer man at sixty. I'd get better at what I do, maybe learn to set out the footings properly myself. That way Terry doesn't need to pay a groundworker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Carol talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly, and whether we could manage on her wage and my pension if I finished at sixty-two. She'd do the sums, she's better with numbers. I'd make the tea and nod.

S3.say: I'd say five years gives the government time to make a plan, so they'd better make one for people my age who can't retrain. I'd say it if asked, but I wouldn't march.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three with the mortgage nearly done, so it's doable if I keep Terry happy. It's tight, but it's not a cliff edge.
S3.do: Tries to overpay the mortgage by fifty a month and takes sandwiches instead of buying bakery lunches. Keeps working for Terry and learns to set out footings himself to save the firm a groundworker.
S3.feel: Worried, but able to see the end of the road.
S3.quote: Tight, but it's not a cliff edge like the two years.
S3.fieldNote: Ben's answer to more time is to pay off the house and get slightly better at his own trade, not to learn new technology. He wants government help for older workers but won't campaign. Five years keeps him anxious but feeling he can reach the finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's loads of time, they'll sort something out. I'd tell the young ones to get learning. I'd say it to Terry's nephew, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, probably. Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, mortgage paid, on my pension. It'll be someone else's problem by then, which sounds selfish, but it's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal, really. Pay the mortgage, put a bit by, keep going for Terry. I'd watch and see what happens to the big building firms, and if they start sending robots to houses like Orchard Road, then I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A bit uneasy about the grandkids, but that's a way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terry's nephew, Kyle. He's twenty-four, quick, likes his gadgets, but he's only ever known building. If robots can do it by the time he's thirty-four, he'll need something else, and he's got a baby coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kyle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get yourself something that robots can't do, though I don't know what that is, son. Maybe talk to Lucy, she knows about these things. I wouldn't pretend I had the answer.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is loads of time and they'll sort something out. I'd tell the young ones, mostly Terry's nephew, to get learning.
S4.think: I'd probably be fine, at sixty-eight with the mortgage paid and on my pension. It'd be someone else's problem by then, which sounds selfish, but it's the truth.
S4.do: Carries on as normal, paying the mortgage, saving a little and working for Terry. Watches what happens at big building firms and would only rethink if robots reached small house jobs.
S4.feel: Fairly calm, with a little unease about his grandchildren.
S4.quote: It'll be someone else's problem by then, which sounds selfish, but it's the truth.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Ben simply aims to reach his pension and mortgage-free home. He's honest that it feels like someone else's problem. His worry goes to Terry's young nephew rather than to himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two years, easily. I'd be sixty with a mortgage and nothing to fall back on. What would help is somebody letting people my age finish on a pension a bit early, or the bank giving us a break on the house, without making us fill in forty forms online.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nobody asks the older ones who came in late. Everyone thinks a man of fifty-eight on a building site has done it all his life. I've done it two years, and I'm still learning which end of the level's which.

headlineQuote: I've done it two years, and I'm still learning which end of the level's which.
portrait: Ben Young is a 58-year-old labourer for a school friend's small extension firm, who came into building after thirty years as a postman. He still uses a flip phone, never touches AI and takes change as weather rather than anyone's fault. He's calm if AI stalls and only a bit uneasy about steady change because small house jobs feel safe, but fast AGI would leave him with a mortgage and nothing to fall back on. With more time, his plan is simply to pay off the house, work hard for Terry and reach his pension.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd be sixty with a mortgage and nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Letting people his age retire a little early on a pension, or a mortgage break from the bank, without forty online forms.
